name: Boston Guildhall
text: Your train passes near Boston Guildhall, on the train's {side}, built in 1390 for St Mary's Guild. In the autumn of 1607 the Puritans now known as the Pilgrim Fathers were brought before the magistrates there, accused of trying to leave for Holland without the King's permission.

name: St Botolph's Church, Boston
text: Your train passes near St Botolph's Church, the Boston Stump, on the train's {side}. Its tower, about 81 metres tall, is one of the tallest medieval towers in the country, long used as a landmark by Boston's fishermen; on a clear day it can be seen from Norfolk.

name: Batemans Brewery
text: Your train passes near Batemans Brewery, on the train's {side}, founded in 1874 by George Bateman, a farmer who sold his farm at Friskney to rent a brewery in Wainfleet beside the railway. It is best known for its XB and XXXB ales, sold as "Good Honest Ales".

name: Magdalen College School, Wainfleet
text: Your train passes close to the old building of Magdalen College School, on the train's {side}, founded in 1484 by William of Waynflete, who also won the town its charter in 1457. The school building is Grade I listed and now houses a museum.

name: Richmond Drive
text: Your train passes near Richmond Drive, on the train's {side}, a cricket ground in Skegness where the first recorded match was played in 1879. In 1935 it held its only first-class match, between a Minor Counties team and the touring South Africans.

name: Spalding Sessions House
text: Your train passes near Spalding Sessions House in the Sheep Market, on the train's {side}, once the main courthouse for the south of Holland in Lincolnshire. Designed by Charles Kirk of Sleaford and built in stone for £6,000, it opened on June 30th 1843, with lions on its buttresses and the royal coat of arms above.

name: St Clement's Church, Rowston
text: Your train passes near the church of St Clement at Rowston, on the train's {side}, which dates from the 12th century and is Grade I listed. Anglo-Saxon carved stone is reused in its chancel wall, and over a doorway in the tower is a 12th-century tympanum carved with a cross.

name: Greyfriars, Lincoln
text: Your train passes near Greyfriars, on the train's {side}, part of a Franciscan friary begun in 1237. After the friars were expelled in 1538 it became a school, the city's grammar school from 1574 to 1900, and its undercroft housed a Mechanics' Institute in which George Boole took part.

name: Guildhall and Stonebow, Lincoln
text: Your train passes near the Stonebow and Guildhall, on the train's {side}, where Lincoln's city council has met since medieval times. The Stonebow, from the Danish for a stone archway, is the old southern gateway into the city, and the Tudor building over it was finished around 1520.

name: St Mary le Wigford
text: Your train passes close to St Mary le Wigford, on the train's {side}, a church dating from the 11th century. The dedication stone in its tower is a reused Roman tombstone, with a later Anglo-Saxon inscription saying that Eirtig had the church built.

name: Monks Abbey, Lincoln
text: Your train passes near the ruins of Monks Abbey, on the train's {side}, beside the River Witham. They belonged to the Benedictine priory of St Mary Magdalene, a small cell of St Mary's Abbey in York, whose lands in Lincoln were confirmed by Henry I in the 1120s.

name: 2008 Market Rasen earthquake
text: Your train passes close to the epicentre of the earthquake of February 27th 2008, on the train's {side}, north of Market Rasen. It measured 5.2, shook for about ten seconds just before one in the morning, and was felt from Hampshire to Newcastle upon Tyne, and in the Netherlands and Belgium.

name: Pingley POW Camp
text: Your train passes near the site of Pingley Camp, on the train's {side}, which held prisoners of war in the Second World War, mainly Italians but Germans too. After the war it became emergency housing; it was pulled down in 2009, and houses now stand there.

name: St Pega's Church, Peakirk
text: Your train passes near the church at Peakirk, on the train's {side}, the only one dedicated to St Pega, the sister of St Guthlac of Crowland, whose cell was here; the village's name means Pega's church. The church is Grade I listed and has a fine series of wall paintings.

name: Stoke Bank
text: Your train runs along Stoke Bank, the long slope south of Stoke Summit. Here, on July 3rd 1938, the steam locomotive Mallard broke the world speed record for steam, at 126 miles an hour; a sign by the line at milepost 90¼ marks the spot.

name: The Northolme
text: Your train passes near the Northolme, on the train's {side}, home of Gainsborough Trinity since 1884. The club was in the Football League from 1896, and in 1911 a crowd of 5,600 saw it beat Chelsea there by three goals to one.

name: Belper North Mill
text: Your train passes near Belper North Mill, on the train's {side}, part of the Derwent Valley Mills World Heritage Site. Jedediah Strutt's North Mill of 1786 burned down in 1803; his son William rebuilt it in 1804 with an iron frame, and it is one of the oldest surviving fireproof buildings in the world.

name: Great British Car Journey
text: Your train passes near the Great British Car Journey, on the train's {side}, a museum that opened on May 22nd 2021 with more than 130 cars telling the story of British car making from 1922 to the present. Visitors can drive some of the cars round the site, with an instructor.

name: Leawood Pump House
text: Your train passes near Leawood Pump House, on the train's {side}, built in 1849 to lift water from the River Derwent into the Cromford Canal. Its beam engine could move almost four tons of water a stroke, and it worked from 1849 until the canal closed in 1944.

name: Lovers' Walks
text: Your train passes near Lovers' Walks, on the train's {side}, on the east bank of the Derwent opposite Matlock Bath. Dating from before 1742, it is said to be the oldest surviving public pleasure ground, and in 1782 it became part of Richard Arkwright's estate.

name: Heights of Abraham Cable Car
text: Your train passes near the Heights of Abraham cable car, on the train's {side}, whose cabins cross the River Derwent on their way up from Matlock Bath. It opened in the spring of 1984, and its cabins are fixed to the cable, so they stop in mid-air whenever another set stops at a station.

name: Tapton House
text: Your train passes near Tapton House, on the train's {side}, home of George Stephenson, the railway engineer, from 1832 until his death in 1848. In 1925 a later owner, Charles Paxton Markham, gave its parkland to the town of Chesterfield.

name: Sheffield F.C.
text: Your train passes near the home ground of Sheffield Football Club, on the train's {side}. Founded in October 1857, it is considered by FIFA to be the oldest independent club still playing football in the world, and in 2004 it was given the FIFA Order of Merit, an award shared with only one other club, Real Madrid.

name: Brooksby Hall
text: Your train passes near Brooksby Hall, on the train's {side}, a manor house of the late 16th century whose gardens run down to the River Wreake and the railway. It was the home of the Villiers family for centuries, and later of Admiral David Beatty, a British commander at the Battle of Jutland in 1916.

name: St Mary's Church, Ashwell
text: Your train passes near St Mary's Church at Ashwell, on the train's {side}, mostly of the 13th and 14th centuries. William Butterfield restored it in 1851, his only major work in Rutland and Leicestershire, and it keeps a wooden effigy of a knight.

name: Oakham Castle
text: Your train passes near Oakham Castle, on the train's {side}, the great hall of a castle built between 1180 and 1190 and one of the best examples of Norman domestic building in England. By an old tradition, peers visiting the town for the first time give a horseshoe, and 230 now hang on its walls.

name: Welland Viaduct
text: Your train crosses the Welland Viaduct, between Northamptonshire and Rutland, the longest viaduct across a valley in the United Kingdom. Finished in 1878, it has 82 arches, and 30 million bricks went into building it.

name: Town Ground, Kettering
text: Your train passes near the Town Ground, on the train's {side}, where Northamptonshire played 65 first-class cricket matches between 1923 and 1971. It saw the county bowled out for 27 by Yorkshire in 1933, and Yorkshire's Bill Bowes take 16 wickets for 35 runs here in 1935.

name: Rushton Triangular Lodge
text: Your train passes near the Triangular Lodge, on the train's {side}, a folly built between 1593 and 1597 by Sir Thomas Tresham, a Roman Catholic imprisoned for his faith. To honour the Trinity, everything comes in threes: three walls, each 33 feet long, with three windows and three gargoyles apiece.

name: Church of St Mary the Virgin, Wellingborough
text: Your train passes near St Mary's Church in Wellingborough, on the train's {side}, designed by Sir Ninian Comper and built between 1908 and 1930. It is one of only a few buildings of the 20th century to be listed Grade I.

name: Tooley's Boatyard
text: Your train passes near Tooley's Boatyard, on the train's {side}, the oldest dry dock in Britain still working, set up to build and repair wooden narrow boats for the Oxford Canal. Tom Rolt wrote about it in his book Narrow Boat in 1944.

name: Kilsby Tunnel
text: Your train goes through Kilsby Tunnel, 2,423 yards long, designed by Robert Stephenson for the London and Birmingham Railway. A roof collapse and flooding made it late and over budget, but when it opened in 1838 it was the longest railway tunnel ever built.

name: Rugby Locomotive Testing Station
text: Your train passes near the site of the Rugby Locomotive Testing Station, on the train's {side}, where engines were run on rollers to test them. First planned by Sir Nigel Gresley, it opened in 1948, made its last test in 1965 and was pulled down in 1984.

name: Northampton Castle
text: Your train passes near what is left of Northampton Castle, on the train's {side}, once one of the most prominent Norman castles in England, built from 1084. The railway all but wiped it out, as the station was built on its site; only the Postern Gate survives, near the station.

name: Wolverton Viaduct
text: Your train crosses Wolverton Viaduct over the River Great Ouse, built in 1838 to Robert Stephenson's design, the largest viaduct on the London and Birmingham Railway. It was widened for four tracks in the 1880s in blue brick, against the red of the original, and the join can be seen from underneath.

name: Glossop Town Hall
text: Your train passes near Glossop Town Hall, on the train's {side}, built in 1838 for the 12th Duke of Norfolk in millstone grit, with a round cupola and clock. Its design marked the change of Howard Town from an industrial village into a town in its own right.

name: Leicester Museum & Art Gallery
text: Your train passes near Leicester Museum and Art Gallery on New Walk, on the train's {side}, which opened in 1849 as one of the first public museums in the United Kingdom. Its first building was designed by Joseph Hansom, who designed the hansom cab, and it shows a dinosaur found in Rutland in 1968.
